title: Learning from the Electronic Structure of Molecules across the Periodic Table
abstract: Machine-Learned Interatomic Potentials (MLIPs) require vast amounts of atomic structure data to learn forces and energies, and their performance continues to improve with training set size. Meanwhile, the even greater quantities of accompanying data in the Hamiltonian matrix $\mathbf{H}$ behind these datasets has so far gone unused for this purpose. Here, we provide a recipe for integrating the orbital interaction data within $\mathbf{H}$ towards training pipelines for atomic-level properties. We first introduce HELM ('Hamiltonian-trained Electronic-structure Learning for Molecules'), a state-of-the-art Hamiltonian prediction model which bridges the gap between Hamiltonian prediction and universal MLIPs by scaling to $\mathbf{H}$ of structures with 100+ atoms, high elemental diversity, and large basis sets including diffuse functions. To accompany HELM, we release a curated Hamiltonian matrix dataset, 'OMol\_CSH\_58k', with unprecedented elemental diversity (58 elements), molecular size (up to 150 atoms), and basis set (def2-TZVPD). Finally, we introduce 'Hamiltonian pretraining' as a method to extract meaningful descriptors of atomic environments even from a limited number atomic structures, and repurpose this shared embedding space to improve performance on energy-prediction in low-data regimes. Our results highlight the use of electronic interactions as a rich and transferable data source for representing chemical space.
problem: Machine-learned interatomic potentials require vast atomic structure data and ignore the rich Hamiltonian matrix information available in training datasets.
approach: HELM trains on Hamiltonian matrices to predict electronic structure, then uses Hamiltonian pretraining to extract transferable descriptors of atomic environments for improving low-data energy prediction.
contribution: State-of-the-art Hamiltonian prediction scaling to 100+ atoms with 58 elements, plus a curated 58k-molecule dataset demonstrating electronic interactions as a transferable data source.
